hints: Focus on the carbon skeleton of X and notice exactly what each Br-bearing carbon is joined to.
Replace each $\text{Br}$ with $\text{OH}$ to draw Y, then count how many carbons are attached to each $\text{C-OH}$ carbon.
Recall what product forms when that particular class of alcohol is oxidised, then check both suggestions together.
walkthrough:
**Look carefully at compound X**

Each $\text{Br}$ is on a ring carbon of cyclohexane. That ring carbon is bonded to two other ring carbons and one $\text{Br}$.

So X is 1,3,5-tribromocyclohexane, with three secondary alkyl bromide groups.

**Hydrolyse X to form Y**

Hydrolysis replaces $\text{C-Br}$ with $\text{C-OH}$:
$$\text{R-Br + OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-OH + Br}^-$$
So Y is 1,3,5-trihydroxycyclohexane.

Each $\text{C-OH}$ carbon is still joined to two other carbons. That is the definition of a secondary alcohol. So suggestion 1 is correct.

**Oxidise Y to form Z**

Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones:
$$\text{R}_2\text{CHOH + [O]} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=O + H}_2\text{O}$$
Since all three $\text{OH}$ groups in Y are secondary, oxidation gives ketone groups. So suggestion 2 is also correct.

Both 1 and 2 are correct.

options.A: Both statements are true. Y has three secondary $\text{OH}$ groups because each is on a cyclohexane ring carbon bonded to two carbons, and oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
options.B: This correctly accepts 1 but wrongly rejects 2. Students may forget that secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones, or confuse with primary alcohols which give aldehydes then acids.
options.C: This correctly accepts 2 but wrongly rejects 1. Students may think a triol cannot be called a secondary alcohol, but classification depends on each $\text{C-OH}$ carbon, and here each is secondary.
options.D: This rejects both statements. It comes from misreading the ring positions as primary or tertiary, or from mixing up oxidation products of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
